item.title: Frame Shifts Come After Edge Control, Not Before
item.description: The right time to move your frames is late. A certified coach only shifts them once a skater has conscious edge control and corrected posture errors. Who then benefits: skaters with an unusual natural stance, such as pigeon toes, or those on tall setups with very big wheels. Everyone else leaves the frame where the factory put it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Flat, Rockered or Anti-Rocker? Frame Setups Explained by Top Skaters. Made with AI.

item.title: Moving Your Frames Treats the Symptom, Not the Cause
item.description: Whether moving your inline frames fixes ankles that collapse inward: usually it does not. A certified coach's answer: it usually comes from too little knee bend and knees drifting inward, not from where the frame sits. Move the frame first and the fault stays. Drive the knee forward and slightly out, over the little toe, instead. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Gear for it on the page: Flat, Rockered or Anti-Rocker? Frame Setups Explained by Top Skaters. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skate Ankle Strap Test: Bend Until Your Knees Cover Your Toes
item.description: A test for how tight the top ankle strap should be, instead of a feeling. Do the top strap up, then bend your knees until they cover your toes. The cuff should hold you at the deepest point of that bend without stopping the movement itself. If your ankle can still tilt inward down there, the strap is not doing its job yet. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. What to get for it, on the page: Should You Size Up or Down in Roller Skates? Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skate Buckles: Your Top Strap Jams Before It Is Tight
item.description: Why you cannot get the top ankle strap tight, and it is not your hands: a one-centimetre fix. A certified coach names the buckle jam: a long plastic strap runs into the buckle housing and sticks before the cuff is snug. The fix is yours to do: trim about a centimetre off the end of the strap so it can travel further into the buckle. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Should You Size Up or Down in Roller Skates? Made with AI.

item.title: Doing Up Your Skates Wrong Is the First Beginner Problem
item.description: Ask a certified coach for the most common problems in inline skating and the first one is not technique: skates that are not done up correctly. A loose boot cannot hold your ankle in line, and every drill after that fights the equipment. Before you blame balance, knees or ankles, check how tight the top of your skate is. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Gear for it on the page: Should You Size Up or Down in Roller Skates? Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Stance: There Is a Wrong Way to Bend Your Knees
item.description: Bending your knees is the first instruction everyone gets, and ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby lists bending them the wrong way among the most common beginner faults. The wrong way is inward: the knees drift towards each other and the skates tip onto their inside edges. The right way is forward, the knee over the middle-to-little toe, so the bend puts the skate on a clean edge. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating One-Foot Glide: Learn the Two-Footed Basics First
item.description: The plough stop is taught first for one precise reason: both feet stay on the ground, and no one-leg balance is asked of you. That is why a one-foot glide cannot be a second-session move. The single-leg balance and edging drills ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby sets are edge work for skaters who already roll: they come after the two-footed basics, never instead of them. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Wobbles: Four Faults Behind Most Beginner Wobbles
item.description: Unexpected wobbles, sore feet, skates tipping inward: ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby traces most beginner trouble to four faults. Skates not done up correctly. Knees bent the wrong way, or not at all. No awareness of where the body is. No awareness of how the weight sits in the footprint. Each has its own fix on this site; the point is to check all four before blaming the skates. Gear for it on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Edge Control Is Endurance Work
item.description: How to keep a clean edge over long distances: edge control and leg strength. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby gives distance skaters two jobs: conscious edge control, through single-leg balance and edging drills that align the knee over the middle-to-little toe, and glute and leg strength built through fitness work, so the knee flex survives the miles instead of fading. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skates Hurting Your Feet? Bend Deeper the Moment They Complain
item.description: Why tired knees straighten and hurt your arches on long skates, and the fix. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby's fix on the road is immediate: check your posture throughout the skate, and the moment the feet start to hurt, bend the knees deeper, forward over the toes. A deeper flex brings the weight back over the middle of the skate and eases the pressure on the arch straight away. Linked on the page: Best Roller Skates for Wide Feet. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Foot Cramps on Long Skates Start at the Edge, Not the Boot
item.description: Feet that cramp twenty minutes into a long skate are usually reporting an edge. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby explains the mechanism: a skate tipped onto its inside edge loads the arch, the foot muscles grip the footbed to hold the weight steady, and the sharp cramps follow within fifteen to thirty minutes. The grip is the effect; the edge is where it comes from. Gear for it on the page: Your First Fitness and Distance Inline Skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Edges Collapse When You Tire
item.description: Edges that are clean at the start of a long skate are not clean at the end. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby names the chain: as the legs tire, the knee bend gets shallow, the weight drifts back, and the skate tips onto its inside edge, pronation arriving with fatigue rather than habit. The posture goes first; the edge follows it down. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Outside Edge: Knowing You Need It Is Not Holding It
item.description: The outside edge is the door to intermediate skating, says ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby, and here is the trap: skaters attack intermediate moves, the forward crossover first of all, before they can hold one. The crossover then happens on a centre edge, which is not a crossover. Knowing the edge is required is not the same skill as producing it on demand. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Edges: Beginners Live on the Inside One
item.description: Every wheel can roll on three edges: inside, centre, outside. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby describes where each level lives. Beginners and advanced beginners have no notion of an outside edge yet: they are still correcting pronation on the inside edge and hunting for the centre. The centre edge is the first goal; the outside edge is the door to the next level. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Inline Skating Edges: the Edge Is the Whole Leg, Not the Ankle
item.description: Where an inline edge comes from: the whole leg, not the ankle, as a rigid boot holds the ankle still. So there is no joint down there to make an edge with: the whole leg leans, knees bent, weight over the wheels. ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby corrects edges the same way: at the knee, driven forward over the toes, never lower down. Where the knee goes, the edge follows. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Crazy Legs on Roller Skates: a Heel Flick That Should Flow, Not Box
item.description: Crazy Legs is the roller dance move that sets you apart from skaters who only dribble or strut; its signature is the funky heel flick no other on-the-spot move has. A certified coach teaches it on quads as one smooth, flowing movement, not the boxy, jerky version seen everywhere, and the method works on inline skates too. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Quad Spins: Equal Weight on Both Skates Is What Makes Them Last
item.description: Why a quad spin dies early, and the weight split that keeps it going. A certified coach says what matters most is weight distribution: equal on both quad skates, so the spin keeps going. Load one skate more than the other and it drags the rotation to a halt. Master the even split on quarter turns first, then let the revolutions grow. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Learning to Spin on Quads: Quarter Turn, Half Turn, Never a Full Spin First
item.description: The stages for learning a toe/heel spin on quads, so you do not skip them. A certified coach builds the toe/heel spin on quads very slowly: a quarter turn, then a half, then consciously adding rotation only once the smaller one is mastered. The technique has to be right with hardly any revolutions before it can be right with many. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: The First Spin to Learn Is on the Toe and Heel Wheels
item.description: The easiest way into spinning on quads, per a certified coach: the toe/heel spin, with weight on the front wheels of one skate and the back wheels of the other. It is the simplest spin to begin with, and it belongs in a dance sequence as much as in plain skating. This is where spinning starts. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Quad Dance Routines: Add One Position at a Time, Then Link Them
item.description: How to build a quad dance routine, per a certified coach: add positions slowly, one at a time, each with its weight placement, and only then sequence them into a short routine. The order is the method: a position you own links to the next; one you are still finding cannot. Short sequences first, long ones later. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Gear for it on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Quad Dance: Learn the Easy Steps Before the Strut and Moonwalk
item.description: Why to learn the easy quad dance steps before the strut or the moonwalk. A certified coach's rule: as in all skating, learn the easy things first and graduate to the complex ones. A skater stuck on a showy move has usually skipped a foundation, not run out of talent. Go back to the simple positions and the hard move gets easier. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. What to get for it, on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Skate Dance Starts With Where Your Weight Sits, Not Where Your Feet Go
item.description: Why first quad dance steps start with weight placement, not foot positions: where your weight sits on each foot is where stability and balance come from, says a certified coach. Learn each position with the weight placed right and it holds; copy the feet alone and it wobbles. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Rock Onto the Toe Stop to Hold Still, or to Turn Around It
item.description: On quads, a skate rocked onto its toe stop is no longer rolling, so you stop drifting away while you stand. The skater behind this site, who learned on quads, names two uses of that stillness: stabilising yourself, and pivoting — on a ramp you wedge on the stop and turn your half-turns around that fixed point. An anchor first, an axis second; never a way of slowing down. Gear for it on the page: Skate Brakes: Heel Brake, Toe Stop or Jam Plugs? Made with AI.

item.title: Push Off the Toe Stop: The Thing That Stops You Rolling Makes You Fast
item.description: The most counter-intuitive use of a quad toe stop is acceleration. The skater behind this site, who learned on quads, says it plainly: you can use the front stop for strong pushes to pick up speed. The reason is the same one that lets it hold you still — without a point that does not roll, you cannot push hard against anything. Plant it, push, roll off onto the wheels. What to get for it, on the page: Skate Brakes: Heel Brake, Toe Stop or Jam Plugs? Made with AI.

item.title: Your Toe Stop Is Not a Brake. It Is a Point That Does Not Roll
item.description: What a quad toe stop is really for: not a brake, but a fixed point that does not roll, says the skater behind this site, who learned on quads. Rock onto it and your wheels leave the floor — the skate is no longer rolling, it is placed. That is not braking, and it is what makes the three real uses possible: holding still, pivoting, pushing. Linked on the page: Skate Brakes: Heel Brake, Toe Stop or Jam Plugs? Made with AI.

item.title: Quad Transitions Are Down, Up, Down With Your Knees
item.description: The flip on quads is quick and safe when the wheels you pivot on are unloaded. A certified coach shows a clear down-up-down of the knees: sink, rise just enough to release the heel or toe wheels, flip, and sink again. The fault to watch: coming up and staying up. Practise both sides for eventual fluency. Quad tutorial from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Quad Transitions: Do Not Swap Your Leading Leg Halfway
item.description: On quads, turning from forwards to backwards is a toe or heel flip, and a certified coach names the common mistake: swapping the leading leg mid-transition. It happens because the end position, the backward scissor glide, is not fluent yet. Fix the end first: glide in that scissor until finishing there feels easy. Quad tutorial from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Hands on Your Knees Until Staying Low Becomes a Habit
item.description: Staying low on skates: a hand-on-knee check, not self-talk. A certified coach uses physical targets instead: touch your knees, or rest your hands on them in a ready position, and run constant knee-bend checks while marching and gliding. If your hands can reach your knees, you are low enough; if they cannot, you have popped up. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Pizza and Chips on the Grass Before You Touch Tarmac
item.description: Staying low on skates: practise on grass before tarmac. A certified coach takes beginners onto grass first: practise the pizza (toes out) and the chips (skates parallel) standing still, in a deep knee bend, where the wheels cannot roll away from you. Then the tarmac — and back to the grass the moment you start rising again. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: You Pop Up Straight Right After Every Push
item.description: Straight knees lock your posture, make you unstable, roll your skates onto the inside edge and set up the backward fall. A certified coach names the moment beginners straighten: right after a push, or during the regroup. Stay continuously low through stride, push and glide — shins into the boot tongue, knees over your toes. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Arms Swing, Shoulders Stay Still
item.description: The arm swing has a limit, and it is the shoulders. A certified coach says: do not twist your torso or rotate your shoulders from side to side. Chest and shoulders stay locked straight ahead, so all the force of the swing goes forward into stride power, none of it sideways into wasted energy. Swinging arms on a still frame is it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Learn the Arm Rhythm on a One-Leg Push Before You Add Speed
item.description: A drill for learning the arm rhythm of skating before you add speed. A certified coach locks the rhythm in with a single-leg push, or the half-lemon drill: one leg does all the pushing, and the opposite arm learns to come forward with every push. Only when that timing is automatic do you build the speed back up. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Opposite Arm Forward to the Leg That Carries You
item.description: The arm swing only works when it is tied to the right leg. A certified coach's rule: always swing the opposite arm forward to the leading support leg, the one bearing your weight. Left leg carrying, right hand forward; then it switches. Get it the other way round and the swing fights your balance instead of feeding it. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Swing the Front Hand Along a V, Never Higher Than Your Nose
item.description: The skating arm swing: a V, not a jogging swing. A certified coach describes a V: the front hand travels forward along an imaginary diagonal and never rises above nose level, while the opposite arm drives straight back and up to make the rear point of the V. Higher than the nose, and the swing lifts you instead of pushing you along. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Arm Swing in Skating: Your Arms Drive the Rhythm of Your Stride
item.description: How your arms drive a skating stride: a certified coach says correct arm use adds momentum, rhythm and stability, whether you accelerate out of a turn or hold speed over distance. The mechanics are precise — a diagonal swing, a height limit, a leg to match — and the next pins take them one at a time. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Hips Pushed Back Show Up as Tense, Scrunched Feet
item.description: Sticking your bottom out behind you feels safe and costs you twice: a certified coach names it among the three beginner faults — it creates lower back strain and scrunched-up, tense feet. The correction: shoulders stacked over the hips, shins bent forward until the kneecaps cover the toes, weight on the front half of the feet, toes relaxed rather than gripping. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. What to get for it, on the page: Best Roller Skates for Wide Feet. Made with AI.

item.title: Forward Crossovers: Hold Two Seconds on One Skate First
item.description: What to master before a forward crossover: gliding on a single skate for at least two seconds, says a certified coach. That is what lets you regroup after the cross without hurrying, without clipping the other skate, and without ending up stuck with both feet crossed — the worst place a skater can be. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Turn Wide and Gentle Before You Ever Turn Tight
item.description: The third cause of a skidding back foot is ambition: a sharp, tight turn attempted before the edge and the knee bend exist. The body panics and flicks the back skate round to finish the arc. A certified coach's progression is patient — wide, gentle ninety-degree curves first, and the arc tightens only as the knee bend and the balance improve, never ahead of them. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Your Weak Leg Refuses to Bend, and That Is Normal
item.description: The second cause of a tapping back foot: the weaker leg simply will not bend while rolling — completely normal, says a certified coach, because your body is not used to carrying its weight on that foot alone. The fix is not a turn at all. Practise a straight-line scissor stance on your weaker side, holding a deep knee-over-toe bend, before you ask that leg to turn anything. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Your Back Foot Taps Through the Turn Because Your Weight Sits on the Heel
item.description: Why your back skate taps through a parallel turn to your weaker side, and how to stop it. The cause: the back knee is not bent far enough over the toes, weight sits on the heel, and that skate's front wheels unweight and skip while you force the turn. The fix: bend the back knee forward until the kneecap covers the toes, squeezing into the ankle strap. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Crossing a Rail on One Skate: Sink Into the Strap, Do Not Hop
item.description: How to cross a tram line on one skate, when the reflex is to unweight or hop the skate across the gap. A certified coach says the opposite: do not lift, sink deeper into your ankle strap for stability and let the wheel roll through. The backwards version follows the same rule — cross the gaps in a reverse scissor with your weight held securely over the trailing leg, never floating. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: The Small Jump Over a Rail Is All About the Landing
item.description: A certified coach files the small jump under intermediate and says the work is in the landing: absorb it with a deep knee-over-toe bend, stay low without ever straightening your legs, and keep a slight scissor on touchdown. I would add: a jump is a choice, unlike a hill, so do not jump much at the start — and when you do, knees like springs, no panic — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Tram Lines: Push From a T When There Is No Room to Build Speed
item.description: How to push off when a tram line leaves no room to build speed. A certified coach's answer for the tight spots is a T stance: one skate set across behind the other, planted between the tracks, so you can push off and keep your momentum where there is no space to build any. Same idea as the scooting push, aimed at a gap. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Cross a Tram Rail Square On, Never at a Slant
item.description: How to cross tram rails on skates: a wheel drops into the gap when it meets it along its length. The fix is geometry: step over the tracks in a wide pizza angle, the V position opened up, so that each wheel crosses the gap perpendicular to it. A certified coach calls these pizza steps and puts them in the beginner's first three methods. It looks clumsy and it works. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Tram Lines: Going Slow Is What Gets Your Wheels Caught
item.description: The beginner's instinct at a tram rail is to slow down, and that is the move that puts a wheel in the gap. A certified coach's first method is a narrow scissor stance with most of your weight — about eighty percent — on the back foot, and speed kept up. Speed is your best friend here: a slow wheel has time to find the rail. Filmed with a street skater in Amsterdam. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Come Back a Better Skater Than the One Who Fell
item.description: A certified coach treats a comeback as an opening, not a loss. Go back to beginner drills — balance, posture, stopping — and use the time to fix old habits and learn the stops you rushed past. Keep sessions shorter and better, and honour any hesitation your body shows: those limits are information. Pain that persists is a question for a professional, not a skating account. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Protective Gear That Actually Fits. Made with AI.

item.title: Your Head Is Ready Before Your Body Is
item.description: Coming back after a fall, the split is normal: your mind is excited to skate again while your body still remembers the impact, and hesitation is a completely natural reaction. A certified coach's advice is to stop comparing yourself to how you skated before. Muscle memory comes back fast. What needs time is the nervous system reconvincing itself that rolling on wheels is safe. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Gear for it on the page: Protective Gear That Actually Fits. Made with AI.

item.title: You Can Stretch Your Sides Without Taking the Skates Off
item.description: A certified coach's side body class is done on skates, while rolling. Simple movements reach the flank muscles that are hard to get at standing still, and they strengthen those muscles at the same time, because the skate is moving underneath you. Done at the end of a session rather than the start, it is aimed at the stiffness you are about to feel, not the one you already have. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: A Stiff Lower Back After Skating May Be Your Sides
item.description: The place that aches is not always the place at fault. A certified coach points at the side body — the muscles down the flanks that are hard to reach and easy to ignore — and says that weakness or tightness there can contribute to lower back pain. Which means the useful thing to stretch after a long skate may not be your back at all. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The Cheapest Thing in a Skater's Bag Is a Ball
item.description: A certified coach ends her foot routine with a massage or myofascial ball rolled under the foot, to release the tension left by skating and to promote circulation. It costs less than anything else you own for skating, it lives in a bag, and it is used after the session rather than before. Nothing about it fixes a badly fitting boot — that is a separate problem with a separate answer. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Gear for it on the page: Best Roller Skates for Wide Feet. Made with AI.

item.title: Tension You Leave in Your Feet Settles There
item.description: A certified coach names a cause of foot discomfort that is not about strength: tension picked up during the session, then left to settle in the feet because nothing works it out afterwards. Her routine strengthens and stretches feet and ankles in the same movements — training balance while it does — then ends with soothing manipulation. It is an after, not a warm-up. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. What to get for it, on the page: Best Roller Skates for Wide Feet. Made with AI.

item.title: Sore Feet: Two Causes, and Only One Is the Boot
item.description: Bad-quality skates hurt whether new or not, a rigid shell always produces some pain, and most beginner foot pain is a fitting problem in disguise — Cass. But a certified coach names a second cause, nothing to do with the boot: the muscles of the feet and ankles are weak, and skating demands intense use of them. Two causes, two fixes. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Best Roller Skates for Wide Feet. Made with AI.

item.title: Hold the Glide for Four Metres, Then Make It Shorter
item.description: The drill that turns a bouncy stride into a smooth one is done in slow motion. Push out on one foot, regroup into a tight parallel stance, then pause there on a centre edge for four to five metres before the next push. As your balance improves, shorten the pause a little at a time, until it matches the natural tempo of push and glide. The pause is the lesson, not the delay. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Point Your Trailing Foot Like a Ballerina
item.description: The second drill of a certified coach's pronation routine holds a centre edge for longer than scooting does. Sink into a deep front knee bend, kneecap over your toes, then point your trailing back foot like a ballerina into a toe roll. Keep nudging the front knee toward your little toes, or the skate collapses onto its inside edge again. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Aim Your Knee at Your Little Toe Until the Wheel Stands Up
item.description: Your skate rolling inward is not fixed by tightening anything. A certified coach's cue is a direction: push your supporting knee slightly forward and outward, toward your little toe, until the wheel underneath is standing completely upright. Practise it while scooting — one leg supporting on a centre edge, the other pushing continuously, like a scooter. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Don't Skip the Lunge Turn on the Way to a Powerstop
item.description: The shortcut to a powerstop is landing on your hip a thousand times. A certified coach's order is the lunge turn, then the lunge stop, then the powerstop — and the first two are not stepping stones, they are useful stops in their own right that you will actually use. Skipping them is how the powerstop stays a fall with a name. Hills past my stops, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: If Your Sliding Skate Grips, It Is Carrying Too Much
item.description: The powerslide, then its one diagnostic. Start in a scissor, transition backward, slide the front leg out in front of you, and lower your chest toward your thighs so all your weight moves onto the support leg. If the sliding skate grips instead of sliding, it is too heavy: the fix is not the sliding foot, it is bending the support knee deeper. Beyond that, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: Downhill T-Stop: 80% of You on the Front Leg
item.description: A certified coach's downhill T-stop, by weight: 80% or more on the front supporting leg, that knee deeply bent, riding a centre edge. The back skate stays light and narrow and drags behind you to control speed — it is not where your weight lives. Finish by pulling the back foot firmly in while the front knee sinks deeper. Steeper than that, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Going Through the Motions Is Not Stopping
item.description: Filmed on a real slope, a student stepped correctly the whole way down and never slowed. That is the trap of the stepping plough: the shape of the movement is easy, and the shape alone brakes nothing. Speed comes off two ways only — knees deep enough to load the edges, and toes turning further in at each step. Past my stops, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. item.title: Turn Your Toes In Further With Every Single Step
item.description: On a hill, a fixed toe angle is why a plough feels like it does nothing. A certified coach's progression: start each stop around 20 to 30 degrees of toe-in, and increase it with every step until you are near 45 at the last one. Sharp inversion plus a low knee bend is what makes stopping force on a steep slope. A hill past that, I ride it out instead — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. item.title: Downhill Plough: Your Knees Must Cover Your Toes
item.description: A student's plough looked right on a real slope and scrubbed no speed at all. The fault was knee bend: from a side view her kneecaps did not cover her toes. Bend until they do, and your legs become shock absorbers that press the edges into the road and take speed out at every step. Straight legs cannot absorb a gradient. A hill I doubt I can stop on, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Heel Brake on a Hill: Sit Down and Push It Forward
item.description: A certified coach's downhill heel brake: scissor the braking foot forward, most of your weight on the back supporting leg, apply and release as needed. To finish, sit down into a deep support-leg knee bend and push the brake past your front wheels. Mine was never powerful enough to stop me and hurt my shin, so I took it off, and a hill I doubt I can stop on I ride it out — Cass. item.title: Inline Skating Downhill: Trust One Stop on the Flat Before Any Hill

Not one you are learning — one you trust. Until then, stay on flat ground. And a hill I doubt I can stop on, I ride it out rather than brake — Cass. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. item.description: Skating for hours with the wrong posture only trains the wrong posture in. A certified coach's check: have a friend film you from a side angle — or rest your phone against a water bottle — and compare your shoulder-to-hip line with a correct demonstration. item.title: Your Weak Leg Needs 100% of Your Weight, Not a Bit More
item.description: Comfortable on one leg and wobbly on the other? That's normal — most skaters load their dominant leg. The fix is a scooting drill: your weak leg is the only support leg, deep knee bend, and your dominant leg does nothing but push. Your weak side carries all your weight while holding a centre edge, neither rolling in nor out. Then skate in a scissor stance with the weak foot leading. item.title: Heel Stop 2: Flip Your Back Skate Onto Its Toe Wheel
item.description: A certified coach's heel brake variation: from the normal heel brake position, flip your back skate up onto its front toe wheel and stay steady by pointing that foot inward. Practise the toe roll first. She says the heel brake works on hills sooner than any other stop; mine wasn't powerful enough for a real stop and hurt my shin, so I take it off. item.title: Inline Skating Stops: No Single Stop Works Everywhere, Build a Tool Belt
item.description: No one stop covers wet ground, a narrow path and real speed. Linear stops — heel brake, T-stop — suit tight spaces; rotational stops (soul slide) let you steer away from a hazard while braking. A certified coach's order: heel brake, plough and stepping plough, T-stop, turn and lunge stops, soul slide. She starts beginners on the heel brake; I took mine off once comfortable. item.title: The T-Stop Is a Slow-Down, Not an Emergency Stop
item.description: I stop in a T myself, and I'll pass this on anyway: a certified coach calls the T-stop an intermediate deceleration method, not an emergency stop — and most beginners rely on it alone. Without a heel brake, you need more than one way to stop. Her pick is the stepping plough: faster deceleration, a true full stop, endless combinations, even with the T-stop. item.title: Downhill Combo: A Gentle T-Stop, Then a Stepping Plough
item.description: No single stop handles a real hill on its own. A certified coach's combination: scrub off the high speed with a gentle T-stop first, then switch to a stepping plough to bring yourself to a smooth, wheel-saving final stop. Or open with a wide regular plough to shed the initial speed and transition straight into stepping. Each stop does the part it is good at. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. item.title: Stepping Plough Mistake: Your Feet Drift Until Your Skates Collide
item.description: The most common stepping plough fault is stepping up and down on the spot. Each step lets your feet migrate inward until your skates clip each other mid-stop. The fix is deliberate: every time you pick up a foot, lift it up AND out to the side, so your stance stays wide and stable all the way to a full stop. Toes in, heels pushing out, and the base never narrows. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: The Stop That Doesn't Eat Your Wheels: The Stepping Plough
item.description: Tired of replacing wheels worn flat by T-stops? The stepping plough is a certified coach's favourite non-emergency stop, and it causes zero wheel wear: instead of dragging a skate, you turn your toes in progressively — a subtle angle first, more as you slow — and reposition your feet step by step until you stop. It also chains with a plough or a T-stop for downhill speed control. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: Lunge Stop, Powerstop, or Powerslide: Which One Comes Next?
item.description: Once your lunge stop is solid, two flashier stops open up from the same base: the powerstop, and the lunge entry into a powerslide. Both start from the same turning position — the lunge stop is the prerequisite for both, not a separate detour. item.title: The Turning Stop Every Quad Skater Should Learn First
item.description: The lunge stop is the prerequisite for two flashier moves — the powerstop and the lunge entry into a powerslide — reason enough to learn it well. Often confused with the easier parallel turn, a different technique. The goal: tighten your turn to roughly a one-metre diameter, which is what stops you. item.title: Build Your T-Stop With 2 Drills Before You Try the Real Thing
item.description: The T-stop looks simple on an experienced skater, but it demands single-leg balance most beginners skip past. Most remove their heel brake and jump straight to a full T-stop — ending up with short, shaky slides. Build it in order instead: a static drill, 80% of your weight on your front leg, deep knee bend, back foot light enough to scrape; then a short rolling slide to build edge stability to a full stop. item.title: Spinning Out on a T-Stop Isn't a Strength Problem
item.description: If your T-stop keeps turning into a spin instead of a slide, it's tempting to blame weak thighs. It's almost never that: too much weight on your sliding leg twists your hip, and your front skate pronates inward. Two drills fix both: the scissor glide, shifting 80% of your weight onto your back leg while lifting the front skate; and the toe roll, gliding on your front leg with trailing foot pointed back. item.title: The Heel Brake Fix Nobody Explains: Use Your Boot as a Lever
item.description: The heel brake has an unfair reputation, usually from two fixable habits: not enough knee bend, and weight on the back of your foot instead of the front. The fix for both — push your shin into the boot cuff, using it as a lever, brake pad in front of your back skate's front wheel. Most who "hate" this brake never tried it. item.title: Heel Brake: 3 Real Mistakes, Coached and Fixed
item.description: A certified coach reviewed a real student's heel brake and found three fixable mistakes. Too-short scissor stance? Push the braking foot further forward. Slamming all your weight down? Keep 70% on your back leg, 30% on the brake, for a smooth slide. Straightening your back knee? Keep it bent, hips over your heel. item.title: The Heel Brake: A Certified Coach Swears By It, I Don't
item.description: ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby teaches the heel brake as the first stop every inline skater should learn — every other method is harder to master. My own experience was rougher: it didn't always stop me in time, left my shin sore, and later got in the way of crossovers, so I take it off now. item.title: There Are Four Powerslides, Not One
item.description: Skaters give up on the powerslide because they think there is one correct version and their body will not do it. There are four. Two ways of turning into it, two legs you can slide on — four combinations, and one will suit you far better than the others. Find your combination, perfect that one, then build the speed up very slowly. Skaters who own this stop say it changed how fast they are willing to go. Still choosing skates? item.title: The Hockey Stop Is Probably Not Your Next Stop
item.description: The hockey stop, or parallel slide, is the one everybody wants and it sits at the top of the difficulty list for most skaters. That is not a reason to give up on it — it is a reason not to make it your current goal. The stop worth your next few months is the powerslide from a forwards entry: far more realistic, and the one experienced skaters reach for in traffic and on slopes. item.title: A Barrel Roll Is Three Moves You May Already Have
item.description: The barrel roll looks like one continuous trick and it is not. It is an assembly of three separate things: a forwards-to-backwards transition, a backward crossover, and a backwards-to-forwards transition. If you can do those three on their own, you are not learning a new move — you are joining three moves you own. If one is missing, you now know which one to practise. Not sure which skates to buy? item.title: Backwards Skating Is Really a One-Leg Problem
item.description: Most skaters stuck going backwards think they need more backwards practice. They do not. Both skates stay glued to the floor because they cannot carry their whole weight on the weaker leg while travelling backwards — so they never dare lift the other. The thing to train is not backwards skating at all. It is single-leg support on your weaker side, which you can build going forwards. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. item.title: You Would Never Skate Forwards Like That
item.description: Watch people skating backwards and you see the same thing every time: both skates flat on the ground the whole way, wiggling side to side. Now picture doing that forwards, both feet glued down, shuffling along. You would call it hopeless, and so would everyone. Nobody notices it backwards because nobody sees themselves. Backwards uses the same principle as forwards: push with one skate, glide on the other. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: New Gear Will Not Skate for You
item.description: Thousands of videos about boots, frames and wheel sizes quietly teach one false idea: that different equipment produces overnight change. Here is the test. Does everyone running a rockered frame have beautiful flowing curves? Clearly not. A rockered frame helps you achieve those curves — it does not create them. Your gear should suit the skating you do, and that is all you can ask of it. Gear for it on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: Wobbly Ankles Are Almost Never Weak Ankles
item.description: If your ankles roll inward, you have probably tightened everything and done ankle exercises, and nothing changed. It is not a strength problem — it is alignment. The ankle drops in and gives you a permanent inside edge. Three things cause it: loose straps, boots too wide for your foot, and not enough knee bend. Speed skaters have powerful legs from deep knee bend, not from isolating ankle muscles. What to get for it, on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: Balance Starts Under Your Soles, Not in Your Head
item.description: Before you fix anything else, learn to feel your own footprint: which part of each sole is taking your weight right now. The sole is a part of the body nobody thinks about, and it is where your balance is actually decided. Practise it on grass, on carpet, even in ordinary shoes — no rolling required. Skaters who build this awareness stop guessing about their position and start correcting it. Linked on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: Take Shorter, Quicker Steps When You Start
item.description: Beginners almost always slow their stepping right down, because slow feels careful and careful feels safe. It is the opposite. A slow step leaves you standing on one skate for a long time, and one skate is exactly where a beginner has no balance yet. Short, quick steps keep your weight moving between your feet instead of parking it on one of them. It feels less elegant and it is far more stable. Gear for it on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: A Wider Pizza Slice Makes You Go Faster
item.description: Toes out, heels in: the pizza slice shape is how you get moving from standing. What nobody explains is that the width of that slice is a throttle. A narrow V gives gentle, controlled propulsion. Open it wide and you accelerate harder than you meant to, which is how a first session ends up feeling out of control. If you pick up speed too fast, do not change the movement — close the angle. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: A Crossover Lands With a Bent Knee, Not a Straight One
item.description: The clumpy, unstable crossover has one cause: the crossing leg arrives straight and only bends afterwards. There is a pause inside it that you can feel. The knee has to already be bent the instant the wheels touch down, front of the kneecap over the toes. Drill it on a circle — a few pushes, then cross straight into a short toe roll, back knee brushing just behind the front one. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Pronation Is Not a Style Problem, It Is a Joint Problem
item.description: Watch a newer skater's boot roll slightly onto its inside edge with every step. It reads as a cosmetic detail and it is not one: left alone, it leads to slow-onset injuries in the ankle, knee or hip on the side that rolls. And it feeds itself, because setting the skate down in a V with the toes turned out keeps loading that same inside edge. Fix the set-down and you have started on the pronation. Gear for it on the page: Best Roller Skates for Adult Beginners. Made with AI.

item.title: Accelerate Towards the Rough Patch, Do Not Slow Into It
item.description: For a short bad stretch, split your feet one in front of the other and coast across it. Shift your weight back towards midfoot and heels so your front wheels do not get tripped by the broken surface, and keep the knees soft so they soak up the bumps. The catch is that it needs speed behind it — so you build speed on the way in, which is the exact opposite of what your nerves are asking for. What to get for it, on the page: Outdoor Skate Wheels: What to Buy. Made with AI.

item.title: On Rough Ground, Raise Your Tempo, Do Not Push Harder
item.description: Bad tarmac takes your speed away instantly, and the instinct is to push harder against it. Wrong lever. What brings the speed back is cadence: short, quick steps set down in a V, barely rolling between them, with almost no force in any single one. Picture the ground as red hot and you not wanting to leave your wheels on it. The same answer works for hills and for headwind. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Linked on the page: Outdoor Skate Wheels: What to Buy. Made with AI.

item.title: A Few Perfect Strides Beat Half an Hour of Sloppy Ones
item.description: The correct skating position is a half-squat, and as a beginner you do not yet have the legs to hold it. So you tire, your knees rise, your backside drifts back, and you spend the end of the session rehearsing the exact technique you were trying to lose. That is the beginner weakness cycle. Do a few strides properly, then stop and rest — resting means standing still, not rolling badly. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Practice Does Not Make Perfect, It Makes Permanent
item.description: The standard advice for a flaw in your skating is to skate more. It does the opposite of what you want: whatever you repeat is what sets. Put a hundred more miles through a bad stride and you own that stride a hundred miles deeper. The way out is not volume, it is seeing what you actually do — get somebody to film you from behind and from the side, then compare it with what you believed. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Leaning Forward Puts You Where Backward Falls Start
item.description: You are afraid of going down backwards, so you push your chest and head forward. It feels logical. But the body moves as one piece: that lean arrives with knees not bent enough and a backside sitting behind your heels, which drops your centre of mass into the back half of the skate — precisely where a backward fall begins. The stance you took out of fear is the one building the risk. Linked on the page: Protective Gear That Actually Fits. Made with AI.

item.title: Body Up, Knees Down — It Is Not a Squat
item.description: The skating stance is not sitting back. Your shoulder stays over your hip, your chest stays upright, and it is the knees that travel forward, until the front of the kneecap covers your toes when seen from the side. Your backside finishes directly above your heels, never behind them. Four words to hold while you skate: body up, knees down. Almost everything else follows from that one shape. item.title: One Drill Takes the V Out of Your Stride
item.description: Push out to the side, then pause in the middle with both skates exactly parallel, close enough to squeeze an imaginary line between them. Push again, pause again. You are not training the push here — you are training the regroup, because the pushing skate has to angle out anyway. Over the weeks you shorten the pause until it vanishes and you are simply skating straight ahead. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The V Is for Starting, Not for Cruising
item.description: Toes out, heels in, the pizza slice shape: that is how everybody gets moving, and it is correct. It is also only for acceleration — standing starts, hills, headwind, broken tarmac. Once you are holding your speed, each skate should set down pointing straight ahead. Most skaters never make the switch and stay in the V the whole way, which gives very short glides and, at speed, becomes a sideways zigzag. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The Spread Eagle Is the Hinge of the Downtown
item.description: Count three of the downtown is a spread eagle, and it is not there for decoration. It is the balance point the whole step turns on: the front cross arrives into it and the back cross leaves from it, so a shaky eagle leaves both crosses with nothing to hang on. Shift your weight fully onto the leg that stays down before the back cross goes anywhere. Learn the eagle on its own first, then learn the step. Gear for it on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: The Downtown Is Eight Counts, Two of Them Standing Still
item.description: Cross in front, cross behind, stop. One, the skates open. Two, one crosses in front. Three, they open into a spread eagle. Four, the other crosses behind. Five, uncross. Six, bring them back alongside. Seven and eight, you do not move at all. Those last two counts are part of the step and not a gap in it — the dancers who look unhurried are the ones who genuinely stop. What to get for it, on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: Forty-Five Degrees Is Already a Real Arabesque
item.description: Height is optional, and that is the part nobody tells you. A free leg at forty-five degrees is a genuine arabesque. Ninety is better. Anything past ninety is for your own pleasure and adds nothing to the figure. The order matters more than the angle: balance first, flexibility second, because a low arabesque held still beats a high one you fall out of. Nearly anyone can hold the low version. item.title: Your Shoulder Blades Hold the Arabesque Up
item.description: Everything above the waist decides whether the shape stays over the skate. Draw the shoulder blades together, open the chest, keep the upper body switched on — a soft back folds forward and takes the whole position down with it. And place your arms from the very first attempt instead of adding them once the leg works: they are not decoration on top of the figure, they are where the balance actually sits. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The Arabesque Straightens From the Hip, Not the Leg
item.description: The leg behind you will not straighten by being lifted. It straightens when your hip travels backwards, as though you were about to sit down on something behind you, and you should feel that pull in the hamstring of the standing leg. Without the hip going back, the free leg stays bent however hard you raise it. Move your weight across through your navel first, then stack head, hip and skate over the standing leg. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: Six Wheels on the Floor Before Four
item.description: The progression has four steps and everyone jumps to the last one. Squat on the spot first, skates hip width, arms out in front, on a beat. Then, still squatting, stretch one leg out while keeping all six wheels on the floor — four under you, two under the extended foot — and pull it back, using an arm to help. That six to four crossing is the step that decides whether you get the move. Only then, one foot, then rolling. Still choosing skates? The page links a five-question quiz. Made with AI.

item.title: Shoot the Duck Is Muscle, Not Technique
item.description: The squat with one leg stretched out in front has no trick hiding inside it. There is no cue you are missing — it is quadriceps, and the way in is repetition. French skaters have never even agreed on a name for it: théière, cafetière, pistolet, bonne femme, four names for one move and no winner. What they do agree on is that the people who can hold it are the people who have squatted a few hundred times. Five questions on the page tell you which skates fit how you ride. Made with AI.

item.title: One Side Trained Is Half a Move Learnt
item.description: Every skater has a side that arrives on its own and a side that feels like week one all over again. Practise only the good one and you have not learnt the move, you have learnt half of it — and the day the ground picks the direction for you, half is what you will have. Alternate left and right inside the same session, deliberately, badly. Working both sides is also what builds the thighs and the adductors evenly. Not sure which skates to buy? There is a short quiz on the page. Made with AI.

item.title: A Straight Eagle Is a Hip Problem, Not a Skating One
item.description: Your spread eagle curves. Everybody's does, and the curved version is the normal one. Holding a dead straight line is a different question entirely: it needs external rotation at the hips that not every body has, and it is not something skating practice will hand you. It is trained off your skates like any other range of motion. Stop rebuilding your technique to fix something your hips are doing. The page links a quiz that matches you to the right skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The Spread Eagle Starts With a Pivot, Not a Stretch
item.description: Both skates open, toes pointing opposite ways, rolling as though they were on a rail. It looks like a position you pull your feet into, and it is not. Come out of a small lemon with the skates parallel, press down on the front of one skate, and let its heel swing all the way round through half a turn. Knees bent, weight in the wheels. The slight curve your line takes is normal and correct. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. On the page: a five-question quiz to pick your skates. Made with AI.

item.title: The Shuffle Is a Wiper Movement, Except Crossed
item.description: Skates a little wider than your hips, heels free, weight on the front wheels. Pivot one skate a quarter turn and bring it back — that is the single-skate version, and it comes first. Then do both at once, drawing them inward until one ends up in front of the other, and alternate which one leads. If a skate rolls a bit while you do it, let it roll. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. What to get for it, on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: The Moonwalk Is One Swap, Made at the Same Instant
item.description: This one is quad-only, and the reason is the brake. One skate rolls on its wheels, the other rests on its toe stop. Drag the rolling skate back until it passes the other, and at that moment both change jobs at once — wheels to stop, stop to wheels. That single simultaneous swap is the whole trick and the whole difficulty. Inline skaters, your brake is at the back and this step does not transfer. The gear that goes with it is listed on the page. The page includes affiliate links. Made with AI.

item.title: The Catwalk Is Just a Crossover Played Fast
item.description: It looks like a step of its own and it is not. Lift a skate, set it down in front of the other, let it travel back underneath you — done slowly, that is a walk. Cross the skate over rather than placing it straight, then run exactly the same thing at double speed, and it is a catwalk. Shoulders back, chin up, weight on the front wheels. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Gear for it on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: The Dribble Only Works on Your Front Wheels
item.description: Skates open, skates close, on the beat: that is the dribble done flat on the floor, and it stays where it is. The version that actually travels is a different animal. Lift your heels slightly, let each skate roll on its front wheels alone, then pivot and swap. It is small and subtle, and it is the sensation that unlocks the step. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. item.title: Roller Dance Starts With a Bounce, Not a Step
item.description: Before any step at all, you find the beat with your knees. Straighten, bend, straighten, bend, weight on the front of your skates and hips forward. That is the bounce, and it comes first because every roller dance step is counted off it. Faster track, faster bounce. Once it holds, let one skate reach out and come back on the count. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Linked on the page: Your First Quad Skates for the Rink, Jam and Dance. Made with AI.

item.title: The Bend Is What Jumps You, Not the Push
item.description: One and two: one, you bend; two, you push. The push takes all the credit and the bend does the work, because without rhythm in the flexion there is nothing for the extension to release. Add your arms and it doubles — they swing back as you bend and come forward as you push. Then land on both skates and set up the next one. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. Still choosing skates? item.title: You Learn to Jump Without Moving an Inch
item.description: Before you ever leave the ground, you lift your heels. Standing still, knees bent, stomach in, eyes ahead — raise both heels onto your front wheels and set them back down, over and over, on a beat. That drill is already the jump. It teaches your quads the work and your ankles the balance while the floor is still doing nothing at all. Quad technique, from Najete Kada. item.title: Going Faster Makes the One-Foot Turn Easier

item.description: Right skate turning right, right skate turning left, left skate turning right, left skate turning left. Four of them, and most skaters only ever practise the one that feels natural. item.title: The Free Leg That Looks Good Is the One That Ruins the Turn
item.description: Turning on one skate, the free leg wants to swing out behind you. It looks good, and it is the mistake. item.description: Nobody teaches the stride as a separate skill, because it is not one. Roll on one foot, bring the skates level, transfer, roll on the other, then do the same thing faster. item.title: Bring Your Skates Side by Side Before You Transfer

item.title: Your T-Stop Wheels Should Graze, Not Dig
item.description: The T-stop fails for one reason more than any other: too much pressure. Shift your weight onto the supporting leg to lighten the other, then set the free skate down behind it and let the wheels drag across the surface instead of biting into it. item.title: The Bolt Under Your Brake Pad Is a Deadline
